ukmt-jmc-2025-01.title: Step by step
ukmt-jmc-2025-01.body:
$10\%$ of $20$ is $2$, and half of $2$ is $1$.

**Answer: (A) 1**

ukmt-jmc-2025-02.title: Count 1111s
ukmt-jmc-2025-02.body:
Top: $4\times1111 + 5\times1111 = 9\times1111$. Bottom: $3\times1111$. So the value is $\frac93 = 3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

ukmt-jmc-2025-03.title: Prime factors
ukmt-jmc-2025-03.body:
$2025 = 3^4\times5^2$. The options are $15 = 3\times5$, $25 = 5^2$, $45 = 3^2\times5$, $75 = 3\times5^2$, $225 = 3^2\times5^2$. Each uses at most four 3s and two 5s, so all five are factors.

**Answer: (E) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2025-03.title: Use 225
ukmt-jmc-2025-03.body:
$2025 = 9\times225$, so $225$ is a factor. Each of $15, 25, 45, 75$ is a factor of $225$ ($225 = 15\times15 = 25\times9 = 45\times5 = 75\times3$), so they are all factors of $2025$ too. All five.

**Answer: (E) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2025-04.title: Count up to 60 hours
ukmt-jmc-2025-04.body:
From 59 h 58 min 21 s, it is $39$ s to 59 h 59 min, then $60$ s more to 60 h. Total $39+60 = 99$ s.

**Answer: (A) 99**

ukmt-jmc-2025-05.title: Subtract two angles
ukmt-jmc-2025-05.body:
The diagonal $PR$ of the square makes $\angle SPR = 45^\circ$. The equilateral triangle gives $\angle SPT = 60^\circ$. So $\angle RPT = 60-45 = 15^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $15^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2025-05.title: Measure from PQ
ukmt-jmc-2025-05.body:
$\angle QPS = 90^\circ$. $\angle QPT = 90-60 = 30^\circ$ and $\angle QPR = 45^\circ$, so the angle between $PT$ and $PR$ is $45-30 = 15^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $15^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2025-06.title: Scale the ratio
ukmt-jmc-2025-06.body:
$36 = 12\times3$, so in the same time Sandra swims $12\times4 = 48$ lengths, i.e. $48\times25 = 1200$ m.

**Answer: (D) 1200 m**

ukmt-jmc-2025-06.title: Distances directly
ukmt-jmc-2025-06.body:
Carol swims $36\times25 = 900$ m. Sandra goes $\frac43$ as far: $\frac43\times900 = 1200$ m.

**Answer: (D) 1200 m**

ukmt-jmc-2025-07.title: Find both
ukmt-jmc-2025-07.body:
The smallest four-digit multiple of $3$ is $1002$ (digit sum $3$; $1000$ and $1001$ are not multiples). The largest three-digit multiple of $4$ is $996$ ($96$ is a multiple of $4$; $997$–$999$ are not). Difference: $1002-996 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2025-07.title: Distance from 1000
ukmt-jmc-2025-07.body:
$999 = 3\times333$, so the next multiple of $3$ is $1002$, which is $2$ above $1000$. $1000 = 4\times250$, so the largest three-digit multiple of $4$ is $996$, which is $4$ below $1000$. Difference $2+4 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2025-08.title: Bars per kilogram
ukmt-jmc-2025-08.body:
There are $10$ bars of $100$ g in each kilogram, so $8.8$ kg is $8.8\times10 = 88$ bars.

**Answer: (B) 88**

ukmt-jmc-2025-09.title: Smallest digits in the right places
ukmt-jmc-2025-09.body:
Tens digits count ten times as much, so they should be as small as possible: they can't be $0$, so they are $1$ and $2$ (worth $10+20 = 30$). The units digits should then be the smallest unused digits, $0$ and $3$. The sum is $30+0+3 = 33$, e.g. $10+23$ or $13+20$.

**Answer: (B) 33**

ukmt-jmc-2025-09.title: Check smaller options
ukmt-jmc-2025-09.body:
The tens digits are two different non-zero digits, so contribute at least $10+20 = 30$; then the units digits are two different digits not equal to $1$ or $2$, so at least $0+3 = 3$. So the sum is at least $33$, and $10+23 = 33$ works.

**Answer: (B) 33**

ukmt-jmc-2025-10.title: Two thirds is 60
ukmt-jmc-2025-10.body:
If $60$ cm plus one third is the whole length, then $60$ cm is the other two thirds. So one third is $30$ cm and the length is $90$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 90 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2025-11.title: Start with the cube
ukmt-jmc-2025-11.body:
One-digit cubes: $1$ and $8$. One-digit squares: $1, 4, 9$. If the cube is $1$, the three numbers are $1, 2, 3$, and there is no square besides $1$ itself – no good. So the cube is $8$, and the numbers are $6,7,8$ or $7,8,9$ (or $8,9,10$, not allowed). Only $7, 8, 9$ contains a square ($9$) and a prime ($7$). Product: $7\times8\times9 = 504$.

**Answer: (E) 504**

ukmt-jmc-2025-11.title: Check by digits
ukmt-jmc-2025-11.body:
The product of three consecutive numbers $n, n+1, n+2$ gives the options: $1\cdot2\cdot3 = 6$, $3\cdot4\cdot5 = 60$, $5\cdot6\cdot7 = 210$, $7\cdot8\cdot9 = 504$. Only $7, 8, 9$ has a prime, a cube and a square ($3,4,5$ has no cube; $5,6,7$ has neither square nor cube; $1,2,3$ would need $1$ to be both square and cube).

**Answer: (E) 504**

ukmt-jmc-2025-12.title: Overlap of two lengths
ukmt-jmc-2025-12.body:
Each square has side $12$ cm. Along the top, $PS = 12$ and $TW = 12$, but together they only span $PW = 21$ cm. So they overlap by $12+12-21 = 3$ cm, i.e. $TS = 3$ cm. The shaded rectangle is $3\times12 = 36$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (B) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2025-12.title: Areas
ukmt-jmc-2025-12.body:
The two squares have total area $2\times144 = 288$ cm$^2$, and the rectangle they form has area $21\times12 = 252$ cm$^2$. The overlap is counted twice, so it is $288-252 = 36$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (B) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2025-13.title: List them
ukmt-jmc-2025-13.body:
Heights and widths: $10\times13$, $12\times14$, $14\times15$, $16\times16$, $18\times17$, ... The gap (width minus height) starts at $3$ and shrinks by $1$ each time: $3, 2, 1, 0, -1, \ldots$ It is $0$ only once, so exactly one square ($16\times16$).

**Answer: (B) 1**

ukmt-jmc-2025-13.title: Algebra
ukmt-jmc-2025-13.body:
Rectangle number $k$ (starting at $k = 0$) is $(10+2k)$ high and $(13+k)$ wide. It is a square when $10+2k = 13+k$, i.e. $k = 3$ – one solution.

**Answer: (B) 1**

ukmt-jmc-2025-14.title: Estimate
ukmt-jmc-2025-14.body:
The sum is less than $3\times125 = 375$, and $6^3 = 216$ while $8^3 = 512$ is already too big. So the answer must be $6^3$, and indeed $27+64+125 = 216$.

**Answer: (A) $6^3$**

ukmt-jmc-2025-15.title: Convert to ounces
ukmt-jmc-2025-15.body:
$8$ pounds $13$ ounces $= 8\times16+13 = 141$ ounces. $141\times28.35 \approx 140\times28.5 \approx 4000$ g $= 4$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 4 kg**

ukmt-jmc-2025-15.title: Grams per pound
ukmt-jmc-2025-15.body:
A pound is $16\times28.35 \approx 454$ g. So $8$ pounds is about $3.6$ kg, and $13$ ounces is about $13\times28 \approx 370$ g. Total about $4.0$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 4 kg**

ukmt-jmc-2025-17.title: Count by bases
ukmt-jmc-2025-17.body:
There are three directions of lines, and a triangle can't have two parallel sides, so every triangle has exactly one horizontal side (its base). 

Triangles with base on the bottom line: the other two sides are one of the two vertical lines and one of the two slanted lines. Each of these $2\times2 = 4$ choices gives a triangle (the big one, the one cut off by the inner slanted line, and two whose left side is the inner vertical line). Likewise there are $4$ triangles with base on the upper horizontal line. Total $8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2025-17.title: One line from each direction
ukmt-jmc-2025-17.body:
Since a triangle cannot have two parallel sides, each triangle uses exactly one line from each of the three pairs (one of the 2 vertical lines, one of the 2 horizontal lines, one of the 2 slanted lines). That gives at most $2\times2\times2 = 8$ triangles, and looking at the diagram, every one of these 8 choices of lines does meet in three points forming a triangle.

**Answer: (C) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2025-18.title: Use the LCM
ukmt-jmc-2025-18.body:
The number is a multiple of both $9$ and $12$, so of their LCM $36$. And $36$ has exactly nine factors: $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36$. Any bigger multiple of $36$ has all of these plus itself, so more than nine. The number is $36$.

**Answer: (B) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2025-18.title: Check the options
ukmt-jmc-2025-18.body:
$24$ and $48$ are not multiples of $9$. $72$ has factors $1,2,3,4,6,8,9,12,18,24,36,72$ (twelve) and $144$ has fifteen. $36$ has nine.

**Answer: (B) 36**

ukmt-jmc-2025-19.title: Fill in the biggest groups first
ukmt-jmc-2025-19.body:
The four P cards need four different numbers, so they get $1, 2, 3, 4$ (one each) – the only 3 goes to a P. The three Q cards need three different numbers from $1, 2, 4$: they get $1, 2, 4$. Left: two 2s and one 4 for the two R cards and the S card. The R cards must differ, so they are R2 and R4, and S gets the last 2: S2.

The pairings are P1, P2, P3, P4, Q1, Q2, Q4, R2, R4, S2. S4 is not among them.

**Answer: (E) S4**

ukmt-jmc-2025-19.title: Check each option
ukmt-jmc-2025-19.body:
Every pairing must be different, so each letter gets different numbers. P (4 cards) must take all of $1,2,3,4$, so P2 is made. Q (3 cards) then cannot have the 3, so takes $1, 2, 4$: Q1 is made. The counters left are $2, 2, 4$. The two R cards need different numbers, so they take $2$ and $4$: R2 and R4 are made. S gets the remaining $2$, so S4 is the pairing that is not made.

**Answer: (E) S4**

ukmt-jmc-2025-20.title: Split QS
ukmt-jmc-2025-20.body:
Let $RS = x$; then $QR = x+1$, and $QR+RS = QS = 4$ gives $2x+1 = 4$, $x = 1.5$. So $PS = PR+RS = 6+1.5 = 7.5$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 7.5 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2025-20.title: Halves and a difference
ukmt-jmc-2025-20.body:
Two lengths with sum $4$ and difference $1$ are $2.5$ and $1.5$. The shorter one is $RS = 1.5$ cm, so $PS = 6+1.5 = 7.5$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 7.5 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2025-21.title: Subtract the corner triangles
ukmt-jmc-2025-21.body:
Let $PQRS$ have side $3$, so its area is $9$. Each corner triangle (like $MPJ$) is right-angled with legs $1$ and $2$, area $1$. The four triangles total $4$, so $JKLM$ has area $9-4 = 5$. Ratio $5 : 9$.

**Answer: (B) 5 : 9**

ukmt-jmc-2025-21.title: Pythagoras
ukmt-jmc-2025-21.body:
With side $3$, $MJ^2 = MP^2+PJ^2 = 2^2+1^2 = 5$, which is the area of $JKLM$. The ratio is $5 : 9$.

**Answer: (B) 5 : 9**

ukmt-jmc-2025-22.title: Solve for the numbers of bags
ukmt-jmc-2025-22.body:
Let there be $x$ bags of the first kind, $y$ of the second and $z$ of the third, with $x+y+z = 12$. Toffees: $4x+5y = 31$. Then $31-5y$ must be a multiple of $4$: trying $y = 0, 1, \ldots, 6$ gives $31, 26, 21, 16, 11, 6, 1$, and only $16$ works. So $y = 3$, $x = 4$, $z = 5$.

Fudges: $x+2y+3z = 4+6+15 = 25$.

**Answer: (D) 25**

ukmt-jmc-2025-22.title: A shortcut
ukmt-jmc-2025-22.body:
Each bag has $3$ fudges minus "something": first kind $1 = 3-2$, second $2 = 3-1$, third $3$. So fudges $= 36 - 2x - y$. From $4x+5y = 31$, the only whole-number solution is $x = 4$, $y = 3$, giving $36-8-3 = 25$.

**Answer: (D) 25**

ukmt-jmc-2025-23.title: Total as a multiple
ukmt-jmc-2025-23.body:
Let $PR = x$, $PQ = y$, $QR = z$, and let $T = x+y+z$ be the round trip.
- $y+z = 2x$, so $T = 3x$: $T$ is a multiple of $3$.
- $x+z = 3y$, so $T = 4y$: $T$ is a multiple of $4$.

So $T$ is a multiple of $12$. Of the options, only $108 = 12\times9$ is. (Then $x = 36$, $y = 27$, $z = 45$, all whole numbers.)

**Answer: (D) 108 km**

ukmt-jmc-2025-23.title: Check 108
ukmt-jmc-2025-23.body:
With $PR = 36$, $PQ = 27$, $QR = 45$: $P\to Q\to R = 27+45 = 72 = 2\times36$ ✓ and $P\to R\to Q = 36+45 = 81 = 3\times27$ ✓. Total $108$ km. The other options are not multiples of both $3$ and $4$ (e.g. $81$ is not a multiple of $4$, $124$ not of $3$), so they fail.

**Answer: (D) 108 km**

ukmt-jmc-2025-24.title: Factors of 175
ukmt-jmc-2025-24.body:
$180 = kN+5$, so $N$ divides $175 = 5^2\times7$. Also the remainder $5$ must be less than $N$, so $N > 5$. The factors of $175$ are $1, 5, 7, 25, 35, 175$; those above $5$ are $7, 25, 35, 175$: four values.

**Answer: (A) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2025-24.title: Check them
ukmt-jmc-2025-24.body:
$180 = 25\times7+5$, $180 = 7\times25+5$, $180 = 5\times35+5$, $180 = 1\times175+5$. ✓ ($N = 5$ fails because $180$ is a multiple of $5$; $N = 1$ gives remainder $0$.)

**Answer: (A) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2025-25.title: One triangle per corner
ukmt-jmc-2025-25.body:
Distances between two vertices of a cube (edge $1$) are $1$ (edge), $\sqrt2$ (face diagonal) or $\sqrt3$ (space diagonal). A triangle with all sides equal must use three face diagonals (three vertices can't be joined to each other by edges, and each vertex has only one vertex at distance $\sqrt3$ from it).

For each vertex $V$ of the cube, the three vertices joined to $V$ by edges are joined to each other by face diagonals, forming an equilateral triangle. This gives one triangle for each of the $8$ vertices, and every equilateral triangle arises this way exactly once (it "cuts off" the one vertex next to all three of its corners). So there are $8$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2025-25.title: Count face diagonals
ukmt-jmc-2025-25.body:
There are $6\times2 = 12$ face diagonals. Each is a side of exactly $2$ equilateral triangles, and each triangle has $3$ sides, so the number of triangles is $\frac{12\times2}{3} = 8$. (A computer check over all $56$ triples of vertices confirms $8$.)

**Answer: (D) 8**
